issues.legal_issue: An authoritative interpretation of existing law applies from the law’s inception unless the Supreme Court expressly limits its operation prospectively.
material_facts: The Supreme Court interpreted the existing rent law to recognize that commercial tenancies were heritable.
The civil court had granted an ejectment decree on the contrary understanding before the Supreme Court’s interpretation.
The Supreme Court had not directed that its interpretation operate only prospectively.
The High Court treated the interpretation as applicable only to cases arising after the Supreme Court’s judgment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not limit the Supreme Court’s interpretation to future cases; the interpretation applied from the inception of the law.
issues.legal_principle: A court interprets existing law rather than legislates, so an interpretation ordinarily relates back to the law’s inception. The Supreme Court may, in its discretion, use prospective overruling to limit the effect of its ruling, as recognized in Golak Nath v. State of Punjab. Dr. Suresh Chandra Verma v. Chancellor, Nagpur University, Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India, and Lily Thomas v. Union of India support the rule that interpretation applies to earlier events absent such a limitation. A High Court cannot impose that limitation. Bharmappa Nemanna Kawale v. Dhondi Bhima Patil did not decide prospective overruling or the executability of a decree passed without inherent jurisdiction.

predicates.case_concerns_temporal_effect_of_existin: The case concerns whether an authoritative interpretation of existing law applies to events predating the interpretation.
predicates.supreme_court_interpreted_existing_law: The Supreme Court interpreted an existing legal rule rather than prescribing a new rule.
predicates.no_prospective_limit_was_prescribed: The Supreme Court did not direct that its interpretation apply only to future cases.
predicates.lower_court_limited_interpretation_to_fu: A lower court treated the Supreme Court’s interpretation as applicable only to cases arising after its judgment.

issues.definition: When a case concerns the temporal effect of an interpretation of existing law, the Supreme Court interpreted that law, no prospective limit was prescribed, and a lower court limited the interpretation to future cases, the interpreted rule applies from the law’s inception.

issues.legal_issue: An ejectment decree passed by a civil court lacking jurisdiction over a tenancy protected by rent-control law is a nullity that may be challenged in execution.
material_facts: The premises were let for commercial use and were covered by rent-control law.
The relevant rent-control scheme reserved eviction proceedings to the rent authority and barred civil-court jurisdiction over eviction of protected tenants.
The civil court passed an ejectment decree on the understanding that the commercial tenancy was not heritable.
The judgment-debtors challenged the decree’s executability in execution proceedings, relying on the rule that the commercial tenancy was heritable.
issues.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to pass the ejectment decree, so the decree was a nullity and could not be executed; the judgment-debtors could raise that objection in execution.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 14 and 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, eviction of a tenant from covered premises could be ordered only by the rent authority, and the civil court’s jurisdiction was barred. Under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an executing court may entertain an objection that a decree is a nullity for want of inherent jurisdiction. Sushil Kumar Mehta v. Govind Ram Bohra holds that such a defect goes to the court’s authority, is not cured by a prior determination of jurisdiction, and may be raised when enforcement is sought, including in execution. Urban Improvement Trust v. Gokul Narain followed that principle. Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar established that the commercial tenancy was heritable; that interpretation applied to the earlier decree as well.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and rent_law_covers_tenancy and rent_regime_reserves_eviction_to_special_authority and civil_court_issued_ejectment_decree and judgment_debtor_challenged_decree_in_execution

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter is an execution proceeding seeking enforcement of an ejectment decree.
predicates.rent_law_covers_tenancy: The premises and tenancy are covered by a rent-control legal regime.
predicates.rent_regime_reserves_eviction_to_special: The governing rent-control regime assigns eviction decisions to a special authority and excludes civil-court jurisdiction over those matters.
predicates.civil_court_issued_ejectment_decree: A civil court issued a decree ordering the tenant’s eviction.
predicates.judgment_debtor_challenged_decree_in_exe: The judgment-debtor objected during execution that the ejectment decree could not be enforced.

issues.definition: When an ejectment decree is being enforced, the tenancy is covered by rent-control law that reserves eviction to a special authority, a civil court issued the decree, and the judgment-debtor challenges it in execution, the decree is a nullity and is unexecutable.
